newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia's ivory trade alive despite seven-year ban.
newsitem.headline: Asia's ivory trade alive despite seven-year ban.

text.p: Illegal traders in Asia are flouting a seven-year-old ban on trade in ivory, posing a renewed threat to elephants, a Hong Kong-based environmental group said on Monday.

"Seven years after the ban, the Asian ivory industry is still in business...and in some cases, thrives," said Traffic Records Analysis of Flora and Fauna in Commerce (TRAFFIC) in a newly-released report detailing Asia's trade in ivory.
"Illicit international ivory trade continues and may be fostered by growing new informal trading networks," it said.
TRAFFIC is part of the network of the international environmental group, The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF).
The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) banned the trade in 1990.
But illegal ivory is still showing up in various parts of the world, said David Melville, executive director of WWF in Hong Kong.
While hard data in the form of seizures is hard to come by, indications show that government enforcement of the ban was lax.
Growing demand brought on by Asia's increasing affluence could threaten the world's remaining elephant population, Melville said.
Demand was particularly worrying in China and Japan, where ivory is used for making signature seals, or "hankos".
"China may be an emerging ivory market, though little is known about the domestic market at this time," he said.
Melville highlighted a legal loophole in Hong Kong, where a five kg (11 lb) exemption for ivory export described as "personal effects" was habitually used for smuggling.
"One such shipment can carry ivory equal to 200 finished signature seals," he said.
"That leak (in Hong Kong) could add up to as much as 20 tonnes per year," he said.
He also called for governments to tighten enforcement of the ban on ivory trade.
"Governments in Asia should make immediate efforts to address significant weaknesses in ivory trade control legislation and administration," he said.
He urged member countries of CITES not to bow to pressure from some African states -- he mentioned Zimbabwe, Namibia and Botswana -- which were pushing to legalise ivory exports.

If they do, this would only open the floodgates for similar demands from other countries and endanger the world's elephant population, Melville said. "If legal trade is permitted, this could have a knock-on effect on other countries," he said.
